metadata.title: Claude, Log Leave.
metadata.subtitle: What a Skill Actually Is
metadata.purpose: Take the log-leave skill apart in the Teardown register: explain the actual machinery (one folder, one SKILL.md, plain-language ordered steps read before execution), name the design trade-off (repeatability at the cost of judgment), and land the carry-out that a skill is a specification Claude reads, not new decision-making authority.

beats.narration_text: Type this and it sounds true: Claude approves an employee's leave request with log-leave. It isn't. Watch 'approves' get corrected to 'logs'. Let's take log-leave apart and see what a skill actually is.

What is a skill?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('approves' -> 'logs') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: Here's what your ear does with 'Claude has a log-leave skill.' It fills in authority — hears a system that decides. That's the natural read. It's wrong. The name is doing the misleading.

Here's the test. Delete the folder. Nothing in the model shifts — no weights change, no authority drains away. Because there was no authority to begin with. What you deleted was a checklist. That's all it ever was.

Here's what's actually inside. A skill is one file. log-leave is a folder holding a single SKILL.md — plain-language instructions, step by step, for how to log a leave request. Claude reads it before it starts. That's the whole machinery.

Here's how Claude runs it. Read the file top to bottom. Work through it step by step, in the order written. No branching, no improvisation — unless the file itself says branch. The file is the program; Claude is the interpreter.

So a skill is a specification, not judgment. That's the design choice. What you gain: the same log entry, every request, every time — repeatability. What you sacrifice: anything the checklist doesn't ask about. Whether the leave qualifies, whether policy allows it — off the map.
Back to the folder. log-leave never gave Claude authority — it gave it a routine. Every run: same file, same steps, same log entry. That's the whole trick. The value is uniformity, not intelligence.

beats.narration_text: Now judge the design honestly. A clean log doesn't prove Claude judged the case right — a checklist can be followed to the letter and still miss what it wasn't asked to check. A flagged incomplete doesn't prove nothing's wrong — it may be an edge case the checklist doesn't cover. The behavior tells you about the checklist, not the situation.

A skill named log-leave doesn't hand Claude authority to approve or judge — it hands it a checklist to read before it starts. Same file, same entry, every run. Anything outside those steps is still on you.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Pick one record you log the same way every time — a time-off request, an expense entry, a status update. Paste this into Claude: 'Write me a SKILL.md for how you log this. Plain language, ordered steps. Then read it back and walk me through exactly what you'll log, before you log it.' You'll see the same trick from the inside — the file is the program.

Walk me through what actually happens mechanically when a skill executes, what a skill guarantees that plain prompting cannot, and name two tasks a skill is bad at and why.' Go deeper: what changes when the same instructions live in a system prompt versus a SKILL.md file — and why did the designers separate them?

llm_exercise.prompt: A skill in Claude Code is a folder with one SKILL.md file — ordered, plain-language steps Claude reads before it executes a routine. Walk me through three things: (1) what actually happens mechanically when a skill executes, from file read to output; (2) what a skill guarantees that plain prompting cannot; (3) name two tasks a skill is well-suited to and two tasks a skill is bad at, and explain the difference.
